Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the UniBank Financial Group Third Quarter 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, instructions for queuing up will be given at that time. Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera:
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to review UniBank Financial Group's results for the third quarter. With me this morning are Johnathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer; Jane Ellis, Chief Financial Officer; Michael Torres, Chief Risk Officer; and Laura Chen, Chief Credit Officer.

Before we begin, let me remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking. These statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a discussion of these factors.

I will now turn the call over to Johnathan.

Johnathan Hale:
Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. UniBank Financial Group delivered strong performance in the third quarter, driven by our commitment to customer service and operational excellence.

Our key priorities for this year remain focused on:
1. Growing our core businesses
2. Investing in technology and innovation
3. Managing risk effectively
4. Optimizing our capital allocation
5. Enhancing our employee engagement.

Now, I'd like to provide some highlights on key areas of strength. First, our fee income showed impressive resilience, totaling around $2.65 billion, up 14% year-over-year. Wealth management led with $1.22 billion, boosted by AUM growth to $1.45 trillion and strong client inflows. Investment banking contributed $820 million amid a tough M&A environment, while cards and payments hit $610 million on volume expansion.

Second, our capital position remains rock-solid, with CET1 at 13.8% and Tier 1 at 15.4%, providing substantial cushion above regulatory buffers and internal targets.

Third, non-interest income benefited from mixed market dynamics, reaching $2.8 billion, up 12% year-over-year, with gains in trading and investment banking offsetting some pressures.

Fourth, our guidance rests on conservative assumptions like Fed rate cuts, steady deposit growth, and controlled expenses.

Fifth, for the next quarter, we see NII in the $2.55 to $2.62 billion range and solid earnings momentum.

These results position us well for sustained growth. I will now turn the call over to Jane to discuss our financial results in more detail.

Jane Ellis:
Thank you, Johnathan, and good morning. UniBank Financial Group reported net income of $1.82 billion for the third quarter, or $1.52 per share. Our results reflect strong revenue growth, disciplined expense management, and a healthy credit environment.

Net interest income increased 5% year-over-year to $2.52 billion, thanks to solid loan expansion and a net interest margin of 3.48%. Non-interest income was particularly strong at $2.8 billion, up 12% from last year and making up 28% of total revenue. Key performance indicators include return on tangible common equity of 13.2% and an efficiency ratio of 54.5%. We are confident in our ability to achieve our financial goals for the year.

Let me expand on some of these drivers, starting with our non-interest fee income, which came in at $2.65 billion for the quarter—up 14% from the prior year and 5% sequentially, accounting for 28% of total revenues. This performance highlights the diversification of our fee-generating capabilities even as we face ongoing Federal Reserve rate increases, easing inflation pressures, and geopolitical challenges in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. Stripping out a prior-year $75 million reversal in cards-related litigation reserves, underlying fee expansion was a healthy 12% year-over-year.

Our three main pillars—wealth management, investment banking, and cards—represented 46%, 31%, and 23% of fees, respectively. In wealth management, we generated $1.22 billion, a record high and up 16% year-over-year, propelled by 8% organic growth in assets under management to $1.45 trillion. This was supported by a 6% climb in equity indices like the S&P 500 and $28 billion in net inflows, largely from high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth clients with more than $10 million in assets.

Recurring streams now form 72% of these fees, with pre-tax margins widening 120 basis points to 42%, aided by strategic tilts toward technology and AI-focused ETFs that capitalized on the Nasdaq's 7% quarterly advance, similar to approaches seen in integrations like Morgan Stanley's E*TRADE. Technologically, our WealthOptix AI platform—a hybrid robo-advisor using machine learning for tailored ESG and alternatives recommendations—achieved 25% uptake among millennial affluent clients, attracting $15 billion in additional flows. Blockchain tokenization for private funds cut settlement periods by 40%, opening up $5 billion in previously illiquid real estate and other assets.

Geographically, the Americas contributed 55% of fees with 18% growth, driven by mass-affluent expansion through digital banking akin to premium offerings like Chase Sapphire. Asia-Pacific jumped 22% via private banking growth in Hong Kong and Singapore, countering flat European results tied to UK pension outflows following the LDI episode. Cross-sell ratios reached 3.8 times, with 40% of new wealth clients adding lending or card products. We aim for 10-12% annual growth through 2025 by expanding share in the $50 trillion global wealth arena, bolstered by deals like our $2 billion acquisition of a Nordic registered investment advisor.

Shifting to investment banking, fees totaled $820 million, up 9% year-over-year and surpassing internal expectations by 5%, despite a 15% drop in overall M&A volumes per Dealogic. We held the #4 spot in global M&A rankings, behind leaders like JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, and Bank of America, completing advisory on $145 billion, highlighted by a $28 billion technology spin-off echoing Broadcom-VMware dynamics.

The mix favored debt capital markets, which rose 25% to $350 million on high-yield activity as Treasury yields hit 5.3%, while equity capital markets fell 5% quarter-over-quarter to $210 million amid sparse IPOs—only 45 U.S. listings versus 120 a year ago. Leveraged finance added $120 million with spreads at 450 basis points. Our IBX Flow platform, featuring quantum-secure encryption, sped cross-border deals by 30%, securing 12% share in Asia-Pacific tech transactions. Generative AI for pitch materials halved preparation time and lifted win rates to 28%.

The Americas drove 60% of fees with 12% growth from energy transition deals, Europe was steady at 20% despite MiFID III oversight, and Asia-Pacific grew 15% on China stimulus-fueled outbound activity worth $50 billion. Our fee backlog is $4.2 billion, up 10% sequentially, setting up acceleration in the second half via sponsor-led buyouts and green bonds. We target top-3 share among 1,200 key corporate clients, with 15% of wins from wealth referrals.

Cards and payments rounded out at $610 million, the fastest grower at 18% year-over-year, on 12% purchase volume increases to $285 billion, exceeding Visa's global pace excluding China. Interchange and services made up 65%, with rewards controlled at 1.8% of spend.

Domestic volumes rose 14% on consumer strength at 3.8% unemployment, international jumped 22% through Apple Card-style co-brands and Google Pay in 15 countries, with tickets up 4% to $85 on travel recovery. PaySecure Next, our AI fraud and tokenization system, slashed chargebacks 35% and tap-to-pay to 72%, while FlexPay BNPL added $45 million in originations, rivaling Affirm.

U.S. volumes led at 70% with 20% growth on elite rewards, Asia-Pacific 25% via India UPI links, and Latin America 16% despite currency swings. Average customer tenure hit 4.2 years, up 10%, with 28% cross-sold to deposits or loans. Durbin exemptions sustain 200-250 basis point margins, and we project 15-20% CAGR via embedded finance, aiming for $100 billion annual volumes by 2026.

This fee profile exemplifies our universal banking advantages—pairing volatile investment banking with enduring wealth and high-throughput cards. We anticipate 10-13% full-year growth, with potential from rate easing and AI enhancements.

Broadening to non-interest income overall, the $2.8 billion figure—12% ahead year-over-year and 28% of revenues, exceeding our 25% ambition—demonstrates franchise breadth in turbulent markets. The S&P 500's 8% AI-led surge, USD-fueled FX swings, and fixed income spreads at 145 basis points per Bloomberg provided a varied backdrop.

In corporate and investment banking, fees hit $1.1 billion, up 18%, with investment banking at $650 million, a 25% leap on M&A and ECM revival. We handled 15 megadeals over $1 billion, like the $12 billion PE acquisition of TechCorp, akin to JPMorgan's recent wins. ECM volumes climbed 30% sequentially via shelf offerings, such as BioPharm's $2.5 billion follow-on. Debt markets grew modestly 5% to $450 million amid 4.2% 10-year yields, but our $15 billion HY pipeline looks promising.

Markets trading generated $850 million, up 22% year-over-year and 10% linked-quarter, with equities up 30% to $250 million in prime brokerage on VIX averages of 18 and 12% Coalition share. FICC rose 15% on Fed signals, commodity moves—oil at $75—and FX options at $120 million amid 9% EUR/USD vol. VaR averaged $45 million, 20% under peers, acing Dodd-Frank tests.

Asset and wealth management fees advanced 8% to $520 million on $45 billion net inflows, lifting AUM to $1.9 trillion. Nasdaq's 12% gain added $120 billion, enhancing advisory fees, with ETF-like products drawing $18 billion, topping BlackRock paces. Alternatives saw $5 billion outflows on PE valuation strains at 15% NAV discounts. Asia-Pacific AWM grew 20% on China wealth shifts, offsetting Europe's MiFID II squeeze.

Consumer and commercial added $330 million, up 5%, with cards at $180 million on 11% transactions despite CFPB caps, treasury up 12% on $70 billion deposits via SWIFT GPI, though deposit fees dipped 3% on digital waivers.

Markets offered tailwinds—equities and vol added 400 basis points—but NIM compression to 3.15% and Middle East risks tempered FX. AI algos improved equities execution 25% for better TCA than Goldman, and IBM Hyperledger blockchain sped trade finance to real-time, yielding $50 million YTD fees.

Recurring sources now 40% of non-interest income, up from 32%, via AWM and payments. Fintech ties like Plaid and Stripe target 15% 2025 growth. Americas led at 60%, Asia-Pacific 25%, Europe steady. Full-year guide: $11.0-$11.5 billion, 10-14% up.

On net interest income specifically for the quarter, we achieved $2.52 billion, surpassing the $2.45-$2.50 billion midpoint. Earning assets averaged $285 billion, up 6.1%, on 8% C&I growth including $4.2 billion Southeast manufacturing under CHIPS Act. Consumer loans grew 3%.

Deposits rose 5.3% to $240 billion, core at 68%. Deposit beta at 42% versus peer 48%, via AI pricing in 1,200 branches. NIM expanded 5 basis points to 3.48%, loan yields to 5.62%, funding costs up 8 to 1.85%. Ex-securities repositioning ($1.5 billion MBS to corporates), core NIM was 3.52%.

U.S. Southeast C&I at 3.85% NIM, Midwest CRE yields at 4.20% on office. Europe flat at $180 million NII, Asia up 12% to $120 million on trade. Cloud migration and SoFi card added deposits; CET1 11.8% supports $3 billion buybacks.

For Q4, NII guidance is $2.55-$2.62 billion, 1-4% sequential rise, NIM 3.47-3.53%. Assumptions: 4-6% loan growth (C&I-led), 3-5% deposits (core >67%), beta 43-45%, no big securities moves. Upside from reshoring, downside from CRE or Fed hawkishness—our $18 billion CRE 92% performing, LTVs <65%. Adjusted EPS $1.45-$1.55, ROE 12.2-13.0%, non-interest up 6% to $1.1 billion, expenses $1.75 billion at 55% efficiency.

Turning to full-year 2024 guidance: adjusted NII $28.5-$29 billion (4-6% up midpoint), non-interest growth 7-9%, expenses $18.2-$18.5 billion for 200-300 basis points leverage, ROTCE 12-13%. Charge-offs 25-35 bps, NPLs <45 bps.

Key assumptions draw from base macro—Philly Fed consensus, stress-tested. Rates: two 25 bps Fed cuts (Nov/Dec), 10-year at 3.9%, curve +50 bps by YE, NIM to 3.15-3.25%. Deposits beta 75%, growth 3-4%, DDA 28% via AI retention; LDR 92-94%, minimal wholesale.

Loans +4-5%, C&I 6-7% (Stripe Capital, MBA mortgage rebound), CRE 1-2% (multifamily/industrial, LTV<65%, office paydowns at 7.5% caps), consumer +3%. IB fees +15% ($2.2B backlog), trading +8% (VIX 18), payments +12% (2M wallets), AWM $450B (+10%, $25B flows).

Expenses +3% ($400M Horizon savings: AWS 70% migration, GenAI fraud cut $150M losses, 25% RPA), FDIC $1.1B flat. U.S. efficient, Europe +5% MiFID, Asia low-cost. Credit: 30 bps NCOs (cards 2.8%, CRE <20 bps), delinquencies <1%, CCAR 'B' 60 bps losses CET1 >11%. CET1 to 11.3%, $3B buybacks $85/share, LCR >115%, NSFR 105%. U.S. 75% earnings +5% NII, Europe fees +10%, APAC +20%. Risks: inflation delays cuts (NII plus), geo/vols (fees minus), CRE vacancies >20%.

I will now turn it over to Michael.

Michael Torres:
Thank you, Jane. As Chief Risk Officer, I would like to briefly discuss our risk management framework. We continue to prioritize proactive risk identification and mitigation. Our key focus areas include cybersecurity threats in digital banking and geopolitical exposures in trade finance. We remain vigilant in monitoring emerging risks and adapting our strategies accordingly.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator:
Ladies and gentlemen, instructions for queuing up will be given at this time. Our first question comes from David Patel with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

David Patel:
Good morning. Can you provide more detail on the fee income breakdown across wealth management, investment banking, and cards, including the main performance drivers?

Johnathan Hale:
Thanks, David. We were pleased with the across-the-board strength there, as Jane outlined. Wealth management's AUM expansion and tech tools like WealthOptix were key, investment banking's DCM and backlog provide momentum, and cards volumes benefited from partnerships and fraud tech. Cross-sell and regional diversification amplified it all. Happy to elaborate if needed.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Sarah Jenkins with Morningstar. Please go ahead.

Sarah Jenkins:
Thanks. Good morning, team. I wanted to dive into your capital position—specifically CET1 and Tier 1 ratios. Could you walk us through the current levels, how they stack up against regulatory requirements, and any trends or initiatives you're pursuing?

Jane Ellis:
Thanks, Sarah, great question. As you know, maintaining a fortress balance sheet is core to our strategy at UniBank Financial Group, especially in this environment of evolving Basel IV implementation and heightened geopolitical risks. Let me break this down systematically.

First, on the headline numbers for Q3 2024: Our CET1 ratio stood at 13.8% on a fully loaded Basel III basis, up 40 basis points quarter-over-quarter and 120 bps year-over-year. That's well above our internal target range of 12.5-13.5% and provides significant headroom. Tier 1 came in at 15.4%, incorporating our AT1 issuance earlier this year—a €2.5 billion perpetual callable deal priced at 6.875%, which was oversubscribed 3x by quality investors like PIMCO and BlackRock.

Now, regulatory requirements: Under fully phased-in Basel III, our minimum Pillar 1 CET1 requirement is 4.5%, with Tier 1 at 6%. But the real story is the buffers. We have a 2.5% Capital Conservation Buffer, a 1.0% Countercyclical Buffer—active in our Nordics and Swiss portfolios—and a 2.25% G-SIB surcharge as a Category 1 bucket 2 bank, per FSB designation. That puts our total CET1 requirement at around 10.75%, with management overlays for Pillar 2A risks adding another 1.5-2.0%. Post the U.S. Fed's Basel III Endgame proposal revisions in July—now softened to a 3.5% output floor from 4.5%—we're modeling a U.S. CET1 requirement north of 11.5% for our Yankee operations. In Europe, ECB Pillar 2 Guidance remains at 1.75% for us, post our SREP review. All-in, we're operating with CET1 excess of over 300 bps, or roughly $18 billion in deployable capital.

Trends have been supportive. RWAs grew modestly by 1.2% QoQ to $1.05 trillion, driven by loan book expansion in high-return segments like U.S. commercial real estate—where we originated $12 billion in multifamily CRE loans at LTVs under 65%—offset by optimizations elsewhere. CET1 benefited from $2.1 billion in organic generation, primarily retained earnings from our 14% ROTE, minus $400 million in dividends and buybacks. We've repurchased $1.5 billion YTD under our $5 billion program, targeting another $2 billion in the second half, subject to stress test outcomes.

Regionally, it's differentiated. In North America, which is 45% of RWAs, CET1 is 14.5%—bolstered by favorable CCAR results and our shift to IRB models for corporates, shaving 50 bps off credit RWAs. Europe, at 35% of RWAs, sits at 13.2%, pressured by higher risk weights on real estate under CRR3 and the €10 billion Spanish mortgage portfolio we stress-tested to a 25% house price drop. Asia-Pacific, our growth engine at 20% of RWAs, clocks in at 13.9%, with tailwinds from Singapore MAS buffer reductions and our digital consumer lending ramp-up via the UniMobile app, now with 15 million users.

On initiatives, we're laser-focused on RWA efficiency without compromising risk appetite. We've rolled out standardized approach tweaks for market risk—aligning with the new FRTB framework—reducing trading book RWAs by 8% or $15 billion. Credit risk modeling upgrades, approved by the PRA and Fed, include LGD refinements using post-COVID data, targeting another 100 bps CET1 accretion by year-end. Securitization remains key: We priced a $4 billion U.S. auto loan ABS in Q3 at 4.75% spread, offloading $3.5 billion RWAs at a 20% risk transfer. And we're exploring more AT1 and T2 issuance—€3 billion planned for Q4—to diversify our capital stack amid rising term premiums.

Strategically, this positions us for M&A and organic growth. We're eyeing bolt-on acquisitions in wealth management, like a potential U.S. RIA platform to rival Schwab's model, funded from excess capital. Stress test resilience is tabled: In our internal EBA-style adverse scenario—GDP drop of 5.5%, unemployment to 12%—we project CET1 at 10.2% fully loaded, passing with room for distributions. Risks? Prolonged high rates could inflate operational RWAs via pension sensitivities, and U.S. Endgame finalization might add 20-30 bps, but our $25 billion CET1 numerator gives buffer.

In short, Sarah, our capital ratios are robust, trend positive, and strategically flexible—enabling us to outperform peers like HSBC or BofA in ROE while de-risking for Basel IV. Happy to take follow-ups.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Lisa Wong with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Lisa Wong:
Can you comment on the credit quality of the commercial real estate portfolio?

Laura Chen:
Thanks, Lisa. Our CRE book remains high-quality, at 12% of total loans and 92% performing, with LTVs capped under 65% for new multifamily and industrial originations. We've managed office exposure carefully through paydowns, with charge-offs under 20 basis points expected. Delinquencies are below 1%, and stress tests to 25% price drops or 20% vacancies show resilience. Overall portfolio NPLs under 45 bps, supported by strong underwriting and vintage performance.

Operator:
There are no further questions at this time. I'd like to turn the conference back over to Johnathan for any closing remarks.

Johnathan Hale:
Thank you for your interest in UniBank Financial Group. We appreciate you joining us today. We look forward to speaking with you again next quarter.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
